Chapter 2. The Limits of Traditional Explanations for Suffering.
When something tragic happens, most of us reach for the stories we've heard our whole lives. Maybe you've been told that suffering is some kind of punishment—karma, fate, or maybe God trying to balance the books. Or, you might hear that pain is a test—something meant to prove your faith or shape your character.
These beliefs get passed down over generations. They give us a sense of order, a way to make sense of chaos. But if you're the one going through real suffering, those explanations can feel like rubbing salt in a wound.
Imagine a woman who suddenly loses her partner in a tragic accident. Her friends, wanting to help, say things like, "Everything happens for a reason." Some hint that maybe there's a lesson in her pain, or that it's all part of some bigger plan. But in her grief, she’s left wondering—am I being blamed for something I can’t even understand? The idea that her pain is deserved, or that it serves some secret purpose, just makes her feel more alone.
A lot of people in pain start questioning these old beliefs. If suffering is punishment, then why do genuinely good people go through so much hardship? Why do kids get sick, or disasters hit those who haven’t done anything wrong? The whole idea of reward and punishment starts to fall apart when you look at real life.
Others lean into the idea that suffering is a test of faith. That can give some comfort—especially to those who find strength in holding on. But it can also feel like a heavy weight. Picture a man fighting a chronic illness. He might wonder, "If I’m not 'passing the test,' does that mean I’m failing as a person?" The pressure to find some hidden meaning, or to respond with perfect faith, can pile guilt on top of grief.
And then, there are those who search for hidden causes. They replay every decision, every moment, hoping to find some reason why things went wrong. It’s really just an attempt to get some control back—as if, by finding the mistake, they could have stopped the pain. But life isn’t that neat. Accidents happen. Illness strikes out of nowhere. Sometimes, there’s simply no one to blame.
After wrestling with these questions, some people start to let go of the need for answers. They realize it’s actually possible to live with uncertainty—to accept that suffering is just part of being human, and it can’t always be explained away. This isn’t giving up. In fact, it’s a kind of freedom—the freedom to grieve without guilt, to look for comfort without having to justify your pain.
In those quiet moments after a loss, what really helps isn’t an explanation. It’s someone simply being there. A friend who sits with you in silence. A neighbor dropping off a meal. A community coming together to mourn. These simple acts don’t answer the big "why," but they do make the weight of suffering a little lighter.
And over time, you start to see that the search for meaning isn’t about finding some grand reason for your pain. It’s about learning to live with what can’t be changed—and reaching out for connection, even when there are no easy answers.
